name: Ivan Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Pryce's, a free-range egg farm. Thirty-two thousand hens in four sheds, and they go out onto the grass in the day. I open the pop-holes, the little doors along the shed, at eight, walk every shed checking for sick or dead birds, then I'm in the packing room with the grader, the machine that weighs every egg and sorts it into small, medium, large. Afternoons it's cleaning, fixing fences, collecting floor eggs the hens lay in the wrong place.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the walking, early, when the sheds are warm and the hens are talking. It sounds strange but you can hear when a shed is happy. What wears me out is the dust, and the fox. We lost two hundred birds in one night last spring because a fence wire shorted. Mr Pryce didn't blame me, but it was my fence.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to work there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My father knows Mr Pryce from the community hall. When I left the warehouse job, he asked him if there was anything. That's how it should work, I think, people vouching for people. I've been there two and a half years and I'm still the one who gets the jobs nobody else wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful, sometimes. I've used it to check what a hen's symptoms might be before calling the vet, and to help my mother read a letter from the council. But it doesn't collect eggs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I carry on as I am, which is not bad, just slow. Mira and I moved in together in the spring, and I help my parents with their bills, so we have maybe two weeks' money saved. That's the real issue, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask Mr Pryce if I can learn the grader properly, the settings and the repairs, so when it breaks I'm not just standing there waiting for his son. Work every Saturday I can. Maybe pay off the sofa we bought on credit, which I regret.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit tired thinking about it, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you help your parents with bills. How much does that take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a tenth of what I earn. My father's knees are bad, he can't work the market stall the way he did. It's not a weight, it's what a son does. Mira understands that, her family is the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you regret the sofa. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I broke my own rule. Don't owe. The salesman made it sound easy and Mira loved it. Every month I see that payment and I think of the fence I should have checked.

S0.say: I'd say it's useful sometimes, like checking a hen's symptoms before calling the vet or helping my mother read a council letter. But it doesn't collect eggs.
S0.think: It means I carry on as I am, which is not bad, just slow. Mira and I have about two weeks of money because I also help my parents with their bills.
S0.do: Asks Mr Pryce to teach him the grader's settings and repairs so he can fix it without waiting for the owner's son. Works every Saturday he can and pays off the sofa bought on credit.
S0.feel: Calm, a little tired at the thought of more of the same.
S0.quote: Every month I see that payment and I think of the fence I should have checked.
S0.fieldNote: Courteous and dutiful; helping his parents came across as an obligation he's proud of. He already uses AI tools now and then, in practical ways. The fox loss and the sofa debt both came back to the same feeling of having let something slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a shame for young people, and that employers should still take on beginners, the way Mr Pryce took me on. But businesses have to do what makes sense. You can't force them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think egg farms have been doing this for years. Ten years ago Pryce's had a woman packing eggs by hand all day. Now the grader does it and I watch it. So I've already seen a task disappear, and I'm still here. That helps me believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the machines that are already there before the next ones come. Ask to go with Mr Pryce's son on the next service visit from the grader engineer. And keep in with the people at the community hall, because jobs come through people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I've seen this already, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened to the woman who used to pack by hand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Okafor. She moved to the farm shop side when the grader came, then she retired. She still comes by at Christmas with cake. So that one went well. I don't know if they all would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if beginners stopped getting hired?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. If it costs less, a business will do it. I'd blame the young people who don't ask, a little. And the schools, for not telling anyone that farm work exists.

S1.say: I'd say it's a shame for young people and employers should still take on beginners. But businesses have to do what makes sense, and you can't force them.
S1.think: Egg farms have been doing this for years. The grader replaced hand-packing and I'm still here, so I've already seen a task disappear without losing my job.
S1.do: Learns the existing machines before new ones arrive and joins the next grader service visit. Stays close to people at the community hall, because work comes through people.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, because he has seen this kind of slow change already.
S1.quote: So I've already seen a task disappear, and I'm still here. That helps me believe it.
S1.fieldNote: His evidence for staying calm is personal: he watched a hand-packing job vanish and the worker move on. True to his market leaning, he wouldn't force businesses to hire, and he blamed schools rather than companies. Relationships, not skills, are his safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government should keep calm and not start throwing money around. People will adjust. Some of them should come and work on farms, we can't get staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, Mira works in the office at the builders' merchant, doing orders and invoices. That's exactly what they're describing. If she's laid off, we're on my money, and my money pays the rent and half of nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tell Mira to start looking now, before anything happens. Maybe the school office, or the doctors' reception. I'd ask Mr Pryce for more hours, maybe the farm shop on Saturdays. We'd stop helping my parents for a while, which I'd hate, but my brother would have to step up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly about Mira, and about telling my father.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that conversation with your father be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Short. He'd say of course, don't worry, and then he wouldn't look at me for a few days. He's proud. My brother lives in the city and earns more, but I'm the one nearby, so I'm the one who helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said keep calm and don't throw money around, but you'd be in trouble if Mira lost her job. How do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They don't fit perfectly, I know. I still think families should carry each other first. But if it's millions of people at once, maybe a family isn't enough. I'd want some help to get her retrained, not a payment forever.

S2.say: I'd say the government should keep calm and not throw money around, because people will adjust. Some office workers should come and work on farms, where staff are short.
S2.think: Mira does orders and invoices at the builders' merchant, which is exactly this kind of work. If she's laid off, my wage covers the rent and almost nothing else.
S2.do: Tells Mira to start looking for work now, at the school office or doctors' reception. Asks Mr Pryce for Saturday hours in the farm shop and pauses help to his parents, asking his brother to step in.
S2.feel: Uneasy about Mira, and dreading telling his father.
S2.quote: I still think families should carry each other first. But if it's millions of people at once, maybe a family isn't enough.
S2.fieldNote: When I named the gap between his public line and his private risk, he thought about it and shifted his view a little rather than defending it. Pausing help to his parents was the cut that hurt most. His girlfriend's office job is the household's weak point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's nothing wrong with people getting rich if they built something. But the crisis is real, and if people feel cheated, they'll vote for anything. I'd say we need calm people in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the eggs will be fine, people always eat eggs, they're the cheapest protein. But rents go up, and Mira's job is likely gone in this one. So the farm is safe and our house isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask Mr Pryce if there's ever a house on the farm, there's an old bungalow by the gate that his mother lived in. Offer to do more security and night checks in return for cheaper rent. Help Mira find anything with her hands, maybe even here in packing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Mira working at the same farm be a good thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good for money, risky for everything else. If the farm has a bad year, we both have a bad year. My father always said don't put both feet in one boat. But in this one, there might only be one boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think should happen with the gains, the share and house price boom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know enough to say. Lower taxes on small businesses, maybe, so they can hire. Not a big new government scheme. I'd want to hear from someone who has run a business, not from a professor.

S3.say: I'd say there's nothing wrong with people getting rich if they built something, but the crisis is real. If people feel cheated they'll vote for anything, so we need calm people in charge.
S3.think: The eggs will be fine because people always eat eggs. But rents go up and Mira's job is likely gone, so the farm is safe and our house isn't.
S3.do: Asks Mr Pryce about renting the old bungalow by the farm gate in exchange for night checks and security. Helps Mira find hands-on work, possibly in the egg packing room.
S3.quote: My father always said don't put both feet in one boat. But in this one, there might only be one boat.
S3.fieldNote: He was honest about not knowing enough to judge the big policy question, and wanted business voices over experts. The bungalow-for-night-checks idea was creative and fits his habit of trading favours within a trusted circle. Cheap eggs give him real confidence about the farm itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks for staying with me. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms will need people for a long time, because animals are not machines. But I'd also say if the robots are good, farmers have the right to use them. It's their business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's already half true in egg farms. The eggs already roll themselves to the packer. What's left for me is the walking, and the hens' business. If a robot walks the shed, I'm the one being graded. I've seen videos of a robot on wheels that drives down the shed picking up floor eggs and checking for dead birds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wait until I'd seen one work properly in a shed like ours, not in a video. Then ask Mr Pryce whether he's thinking about it, and ask to be the one who looks after it if he buys one. If he says no to me, start looking at the warehouse jobs again, though they'll be robots too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Close to alarmed when I think about the warehouses as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your father say about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That a man must work, robot or no robot. He'd tell me to go and ask Mr Pryce straight away and not wait. He'd be right. He's always right about the asking part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your work do you think a robot couldn't do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hearing the shed. When the hens go quiet in the wrong way, you know before you see anything. Maybe a machine with a microphone could learn it. I hope it takes a long time.

S4.say: I'd say farms will need people for a long time, because animals are not machines. But if robots are good, farmers have the right to use them, since it's their business.
S4.think: It's already half true on egg farms, because the eggs roll themselves to the packer. What's left for me is walking the sheds, and a robot that does that would make me the one being graded.
S4.do: Waits to see a robot work in a real shed, then asks Mr Pryce directly about his plans and asks to be the one who looks after it. Looks at warehouse jobs again if the answer is no.
S4.feel: Anxious, close to alarmed once he remembers the warehouses are changing too.
S4.quote: The eggs already roll themselves to the packer. What's left for me is the walking, and the hens' business. If a robot walks the shed, I'm the one being graded.
S4.fieldNote: He defended the owner's right to use robots even while describing exactly how he'd be replaced, a very consistent free-market view. His fallback, the warehouse, is also on the card, and he noticed that himself. His father's advice to ask straight away is his compass.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, because my fallback goes too. What would help is if farms that buy robots got a tax break for keeping one person on to run them and train them. Not a handout, a reason to keep people. And for families to be able to rent near where they work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the hens. People buy free-range because they picture a person looking after them. If it's all machines, will they still pay extra? I don't know. That might be what saves us.

headlineQuote: The eggs already roll themselves to the packer. What's left for me is the walking, and the hens' business. If a robot walks the shed, I'm the one being graded.
portrait: Ivan Haddad is a 27-year-old junior on a 32,000-hen free-range egg farm, who got the job because his father vouched for him at the community hall. He lives with his partner Mira, who works in a builders' merchant office, helps his parents with their bills, and has about two weeks of savings. He uses AI tools now and then and stays calm through the slower scenarios because he has already watched a grading machine replace hand-packing. His worry shifts to Mira's office job and their rent as AI speeds up. With robots he sees how exactly he'd be replaced, yet still defends an owner's right to use them, and wants tax breaks for keeping people on rather than handouts.
biggestWorry: The fast robots scenario, because both his farm job and his fallback in warehouse work would be at risk.
whatWouldHelp: A tax break for farms that keep a person on to run and train robots, and affordable rents near where people work.
